recipe.byline: Dana Whitfield · Night nurse for twelve years
recipe.title: Bringing a parent home: is the medicine list clear?
recipe.intro: Did your parent just come home from the hospital with a new list of pills? Answer a few quick questions to see where things stand and what to ask next.

questions.text: Do you have the written discharge medicine list?

options.label: No, nothing in writing
options.why: Without the list you can't sort anything out, so ask the hospital or the pharmacy for it today.

options.label: Not sure
options.why: Families are often handed a stack of papers, and it matters which one is the actual medicine list.

questions.text: Do you know which new pills replace the ones your parent already had?

options.label: Yes, it was explained and I understand it
Some of them, not all
options.why: The pills you're unsure about are the ones to bring to the pharmacist first.

options.label: No idea
options.why: This is where families most often go wrong, so call the pharmacist or the discharging team before guessing.

questions.text: Are there old bottles at home that might overlap with the new list?

options.label: Yes, and I haven't checked them yet
options.why: Old bottles sitting next to new ones are how the same medicine can end up taken twice.

options.label: Not sure
options.why: You can't tell what is new and what has been replaced until everything at home is in one place.

questions.text: Has a pharmacist gone through the full list with you?

options.label: Not yet
options.why: A pharmacist can check every prescription together and spot overlaps, so it's worth asking for a review.

questions.text: Do you know who to call with a medicine question at night or on a weekend?

options.label: No
options.why: Questions about the list often come up in the middle of the night, so find the number before you need it.

options.label: Not sure
options.why: If you don't know who answers after hours, you'll be left guessing when a question comes up.

questions.text: Since coming home, has your parent had new symptoms, such as being very drowsy, confused or falling?

options.label: Yes
options.why: New symptoms need a doctor or pharmacist now, not a checklist; in an emergency, call emergency services.

stop.title: Stop. Get help today.
stop.body: At least one answer means you need help now, not later. Call the pharmacist, the prescriber or the hospital team that discharged your parent, and in an emergency call emergency services. Don't stop or change any medicine on your own.

unclear.title: You can't judge this yet.
unclear.body: There are a few things you don't know yet, and they matter. Find the written list, gather every bottle in one place and take your questions to the pharmacist.

clear.title: Nothing alarming so far.
clear.body: From your answers, the list looks under control for now. Keep the list and the bottles together, and check again whenever a medicine changes.

always: Keep the discharge list and every medicine bottle together in one place.
Write down your questions as they come up, and bring them to the pharmacist.
Never stop or change a medicine without asking the prescriber or pharmacist first.
recipe.disclaimer: This is general guidance from one nurse's experience to help you get organised. It is not medical advice or a review of your parent's medicines, so always check with a pharmacist or doctor.

method.name: The Discharge List Walkthrough
method.oneLine: A plain way for families to line up the new discharge list against the medicines already at home, so they know what is unclear and who to ask.

steps.name: Get the list in hand
steps.text: Make sure you have the written discharge medicine list before you try to sort anything out.

steps.name: Line up old and new
steps.text: Put the new list next to the bottles already at home and see which ones look like they overlap.

steps.name: Mark what is unclear
steps.text: Circle every pill where you can't tell whether it replaces an old one, adds to it or stays the same.

steps.name: Take it to the pharmacist
steps.text: Bring the marked list and the bottles to the pharmacist or the prescriber and ask your questions there.

method.limits: It helps families get organised and ask better questions. It never says which medicine to take, stop or change, and it does not replace a pharmacist's review or a doctor's instructions.
